Threat.value: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

vignette: The memory of that room never arrived as a narrative. It came as a sequence of frozen frames: the cracked linoleum beneath his knees, the yellowed face of a man leaning over him, the slow drip of something sharp smelling from a rusted pipe. At fifty-three, Tane Kalani, a Pacific American commercial pilot, could still feel the phantom bite of steel restraints, the way the air in that concrete box had turned thick with the smell of damp wool and copper. He had come to believe that the guards' sudden stillness meant the next strike was coming. When they stopped talking, the quiet was not peaceful; it was the intake of breath before pain. He had also learned that pleading, that shedding tears, only made them lean closer, amused by his breaking composure. The violation of it-the sheer, pointless cruelty-had etched itself into his nervous system. He survived by staying rigid, by watching every shift in posture, every glance that might mean mercy or a new instrument. When he returned to his career, the world no longer felt safe simply because it looked familiar. Habits formed slowly, like salt on glass. He began checking the flight deck doors, the galley latches, the cabin secure indicators with the same methodical pressure he used to verify fuel loads. At home, he would walk the perimeter of their suburban house, turning every deadbolt three times, peering through the blinds until the locks clicked into place and his chest unclenched. He was certain that securing the perimeter was the only way to guarantee safety. In the air, the cockpit became his controlled territory. When the cabin went quiet during cruise, the sudden drop in engine hum and chatter made his hands tighten on the yoke. What frightened him most was the unbroken quiet; it felt like a held breath, a precursor to sudden violence. He found himself scanning the rows behind him, watching shoulders slump, eyes widen, mouths part in unexpected ways. He was reading for threats, for the flash of aggression that had once preceded the worst of it. The smell of jet fuel and stale coffee occasionally rose in the galley. A flash would snap into place-a man's boots on wet concrete, a rusted chain hanging from a hook-and the emotion would rise so fast it choked his throat. He could not afford to stop mid-flight, but in the brief pauses between sectors, he would step away, press his forehead against the cold bulkhead, and wait for the flood to pass. The outside world grew narrower. He avoided the terminal lounges on layovers, sticking to quiet corridors where the air moved in straight lines. He remembered a briefing in Seattle where a younger co-pilot wept quietly over a divorce paper. Tane had stood rigid, the image of his own forced compliance flashing behind his eyes. He could not bear the sound of uncontrolled weeping; it felt like a summons to his own powerlessness. He also grew sharply attuned to how people treated each other. A loud argument in a hotel lobby, a supervisor snapping at a ground crew member, a passenger cutting across a queue-these were not just inconveniences. They were violations that pulled at a raw nerve. He would leave the room, citing a sudden headache, because the breach of decency mirrored the utter lawlessness of the place where he had been kept. Over time, the parallel weight of these habits had reshaped his daily life. He had stepped down from the left seat, trading cockpit windows for a desk in airport operations. His wife noticed the distance, the way he flinched when the television turned on too quietly, the way he stopped flying altogether because the sudden drop in altitude felt like a trap closing. She had begged him to speak to someone, not for the airline, but for himself. Now, sitting in the therapist's office, Tane stared at his hands. He was not afraid of the memories themselves; he was afraid of losing control when they returned, of the silence that always preceded the worst of it, of the way his own body had turned into a warning system that never slept. He had come to the clinic because his wife's quiet plea had finally outpaced his fear. He hoped, more than he dared say, that he might learn to sit through a conversation without scanning the exit, to let a room fill with noise without bracing for impact, and to finally stop checking the locks.
